Most small producers grow by selling directly: WhatsApp orders, Instagram DMs, a market stall, friends at church or work. Direct selling gives you the full price and close contact with buyers, but it has a ceiling. You can only sell to the people who already find you, and every sale needs your time. **Distribution** means building routes to buyers you would never reach alone, through businesses and people who already have those buyers' trust and attention.

This course is for producers who already sell steadily and now want to go further: into shops, supermarkets, pharmacies, online marketplaces, distributors and agent networks. It assumes you already have a product, a label and a cost price. Here you learn how to choose channels, protect your brand when other people sell it, and check that each channel truly makes money.

Channel concentration: how exposed are you?

Before adding anything new, measure what you have. **Channel concentration** is how much of your revenue depends on one channel. If one channel brings most of your money, a single disruption (your Instagram account is hacked, the market is closed for repairs, a salon owner relocates) cuts most of your income overnight. Spreading sales across two or three healthy channels makes the business steadier.
Worked example: measuring channel share
For example, Amaka makes whipped shea body butter in 250 g jars in Abuja. Her direct price is about 4,000 naira (approximate). Last month she sold 400 jars.
WhatsApp and Instagram orders: 260 jars x 4,000 = 1,040,000 naira.
Saturday market stall: 100 jars x 4,000 = 400,000 naira.
One salon that buys from her at 2,800 naira a jar: 40 jars x 2,800 = 112,000 naira.
Two thirds of Amaka's income depends on her phone and social media accounts. Her expansion goal is not just more sales but a better spread, so that no single channel can sink the month.

Notice that the salon brings only 7.2% of revenue but 10% of the jars (40 of 400). Units and naira tell different stories because the salon pays a lower price. Always look at both, and later you will add a third view: profit per channel.
Use real records, not memory

Take the figures from your sales book, WhatsApp order list or bank and POS statements for the last one to three months. Memory usually overestimates the channel you enjoy most and forgets small, regular buyers.
Three shifts that come with distribution
**From one channel to several working together.** Your social media can send buyers to the shops that stock you, and shop presence makes your online brand look established.
**From a personal brand to a product brand.** Today many customers buy because they know you. On a supermarket shelf your jar must sell itself through its name, label, price and quality.
**From selling every unit to enabling others to sell.** Your job moves towards supplying, training, invoicing and checking, rather than chatting to every buyer.

None of these shifts happens by accident. A producer who rushes into five shops at once often runs out of stock, chases unpaid invoices and lets quality slip, and the brand suffers. The rest of this course gives you a careful order: measure, check readiness, set your rules, build simple systems, run the numbers, then pitch and grow one channel at a time.

Capacity: do the maths before you say yes
Worked example: can she supply a pharmacy chain?

For example, Amaka (from the last lesson) makes about 400 jars a month and can stretch to 500 with her current kitchen, equipment and two helpers. A pharmacy chain with 4 branches asks for 24 jars per branch every two weeks.
Monthly demand from the chain: 4 branches x 24 jars x 2 deliveries = 192 jars.
New total demand: 400 existing + 192 = 592 jars a month.
Gap: 592 - 500 maximum = 92 jars short every month.

Cash tied up: if each jar costs her about 1,900 naira (approximate) to make and the chain pays 30 days after delivery, she must fund at least 192 x 1,900 = 364,800 naira of stock before the first payment arrives.
Options: start with 2 branches (96 jars a month, total 496, within capacity), add a production day, or delay until she has the cash.

Amaka agrees to start with 2 branches. She stays within capacity, needs about 182,400 naira (96 x 1,900) of working cash instead of 364,800, and can add branches once the first two prove the product sells.
Never starve your loyal buyers
If a new channel takes stock your direct customers were waiting for, you trade a known, full-price customer for an unproven, lower-price one. Protect existing demand first, then add.
Matching the channel to your product

Different channels suit different products. Ask four questions: Does the product sell on sight, or does it need explaining? Is it fragile, heavy or perishable? How long is its shelf life? Is the price high enough to carry another party's margin?
**Shops and supermarkets** suit products that sell on sight, have a good shelf life and look strong next to competing brands.
**Online marketplaces** suit products that photograph well, survive courier delivery and have a clear size or variant.
**Agents and resellers** suit products that benefit from a personal recommendation, a demonstration or local trust.
**Distributors** suit products with steady demand across many shops, where you can afford a further margin layer.

When other people sell your product, they carry your reputation. A customer who buys a jar from a pharmacy does not know or care that the pharmacist stored it beside a hot window; she only knows the butter was runny. Your protection is to decide, in writing, what must never change, and to agree it clearly with every partner.
Two people with a signed agreement
A short written agreement prevents most of the misunderstandings that end distribution relationships.
Your brand standards sheet
A **brand standards sheet** is one page that answers: what does a customer get, every time, wherever she buys? Keep it practical, not a slogan.
**Product:** the recipe or method, net weight or volume, and the quality checks each batch must pass.
**Packaging:** the exact container, lid, label design and colours; no handwritten or photocopied labels.
**Price:** your recommended retail price (RRP) for each size and your trade price for each type of partner.
**Presentation:** approved product photos and a short, honest description partners may use. No health or medical claims you cannot support.
**Storage and handling:** for example, keep below 30 °C and out of direct sunlight, if that is what your product needs.
**Customer care:** who handles complaints and how quickly.
Price rules: RRP, floor price and parity

Set a **recommended retail price** so a customer sees roughly the same price wherever she shops. Then set your **floor price**, the lowest trade price you will accept for each pack size. Work it out from your costs, not from a buyer's pressure: if a jar costs you 1,900 naira and you need at least 25% margin on what you receive, the floor is 1,900 / 0.75 = about 2,533 naira. Any deal below that loses you the profit you need.

Keep **price parity**: do not sell direct on Instagram far below the RRP your shops are charging. If a pharmacy sells at 4,000 naira and you sell at 3,200 online, the pharmacy loses customers to you and soon stops reordering. Run direct promotions carefully and tell partners in advance.
What every agreement should cover
Agreement terms checklist
Products, sizes and trade prices
Order minimum and delivery
Payment terms and method
Outright or consignment stock
Returns, damage and expiry

If a term is not written down, each side remembers it differently, so cover all six before the first delivery.

**Outright purchase** means the shop buys the stock and owns it; unsold units are its problem unless you agree otherwise. **Consignment** means you still own the stock on the shelf, and the shop pays only for what it sells after each count. Consignment is easier to get into a shop but riskier for you: write down who pays for damaged or missing units, how often you count, and how quickly payment follows the count.

Also cover **exclusivity and territory** if a partner asks for them. A distributor may want to be your only supplier in Kano, for example. Agree to exclusivity only for a limited period, a defined area and with a minimum order level, so you are not locked into a partner who stops buying.
Worked example: a one-page supply agreement
For example, Amaka agrees terms with a pharmacy owner in Garki for her 250 g shea butter.
Product and price: 250 g jar at a trade price of 2,800 naira; RRP 4,000 naira, so the pharmacy keeps 1,200 naira, a 30% margin on the shelf price.
Order: minimum 12 jars, delivered within 3 working days of a WhatsApp order.
Payment: outright purchase, paid by bank transfer to her business account within 14 days of delivery.
Returns: jars damaged in delivery replaced at her cost if reported within 48 hours; no returns for jars kept in heat or past their best-before date.
Review: both sides review sales and terms after 8 weeks; either side may end with 2 weeks' written notice by WhatsApp or email.
Both signed a one-page sheet and each kept a photo. When a jar arrived cracked, the 48-hour rule settled it in one message instead of an argument.
Simple, but still serious
A one-page agreement signed by both sides is far better than a verbal deal. For larger contracts, exclusivity, or anything involving big sums, have a lawyer review the document before you sign.
Know your walk-away point

Before any negotiation, write your **walk-away point**: the deal you would rather refuse than accept. Negotiators call your best alternative if talks fail your BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement). If your alternative is selling those same 96 jars to your own customers at full price, a buyer demanding a 50% discount and 90-day credit has a weak offer, and you can say no politely.

Pressure usually comes in three forms: a deeper discount for a bigger order, longer credit, or a cheaper ingredient to hit a lower price. Answer each from your sheet. A bigger order can earn a small volume discount only if your floor price still holds. Longer credit needs a price that covers the cost of waiting. A cheaper recipe changes the product your customers trust, so it stays off the table.

Writing a short SOP

A **standard operating procedure (SOP)** is a numbered list anyone on your team can follow without asking you. Keep it to one page per channel, written in the words your helpers use. Here is an example for outright retail orders.
When a shop orders on WhatsApp, reply within 2 hours confirming items, quantities, price and delivery day.
Enter the order in the order log with an order number, for example GK-014.
Pick jars from the oldest batch first, check each label and seal, and pack in a carton with padding.
Prepare two copies of the delivery note and one invoice showing order number, quantities, prices, total and payment due date.
At delivery, count together with the shop staff; both sign both delivery notes; leave one, bring one back.
Photograph the signed note and save it in the shop's WhatsApp chat and in your records folder.
One day before the due date, send a polite reminder with the invoice attached; record the payment the day it arrives.
Credit terms and your cash cycle

**Net 30** means the partner pays 30 days after the invoice date. It sounds harmless, but you paid for ingredients and jars well before you delivered. Count the days from when cash leaves your hands to when it comes back. This is your **cash cycle**.
Worked example: how long is the cash tied up?

For example, Amaka buys shea butter, oils and jars on 10 September for a 48-jar order from a distributor in Kaduna. Her cost is about 1,900 naira (approximate) per jar. The distributor pays net 30 from delivery.
Cash out on 10 September: 48 x 1,900 = 91,200 naira for materials and labour.
She makes, cures and labels the jars, and delivers on 25 September (15 days later).
Payment is due 30 days after delivery: 25 October.
Cash cycle: 15 days of production + 30 days of credit = 45 days.
If the distributor pays 10 days late, the cycle becomes 55 days.

Amaka needs 91,200 naira of her own money locked away for about six to eight weeks per order. Before agreeing to a second distributor, she checks that she has enough working cash for both cycles at once.
Payment safety

Take partner payments only into your business account, never into a helper's or agent's personal account. Confirm every transfer in your banking app before releasing stock, because fake transfer alerts and screenshots are a common fraud. Never share your banking PIN or one-time passwords with anyone.
Your order and payment log

A simple Google Sheet with one row per order is enough. Use these columns: order number, date, partner, channel, product and quantity, invoice value, due date, date paid, amount paid, balance and notes. Add a filter so you can see everything unpaid, sorted by due date. Each Monday, look at the unpaid list and send reminders. A business that is owed a lot of money by partners can be profitable on paper and still unable to buy materials.

For marketplaces, also record the payout you actually received for each order, since fees and returns mean it is often less than the listed price. For agents, record stock issued to each agent, units sold, cash paid in and commission paid out, so that at any moment you know who holds your stock and your money.
Review channels on a fixed date

Put a review in your calendar three months after opening each new channel. Look at orders, on-time payment and returns. A fixed date stops you from quitting too early in frustration or hanging on for a year out of hope.

At your stall, you can see if a jar looks wrong before a customer picks it up. In a shop forty kilometres away, you cannot. Quality across channels depends on three habits: knowing which batch went where, making sure old stock sells before new stock, and treating every complaint as information to trace and fix.
A sealed cardboard package
Each carton you dispatch should be traceable to the batch it came from.
Batch codes and a batch record

A **batch code** is a short label that identifies when and how a group of products was made. A simple format is product, date and batch number for that day: for example **SB-2409-02** means shea butter, made in September 2024 (24-09), second batch of the day. Print or stamp it on every jar alongside the best-before date.

Keep a **batch record** for each code: date, ingredients used and their supplier lot numbers if available, quantity made, who made it, quality checks done, and where every unit went. If your product is NAFDAC-registered, the product you supply must match what was registered; speak to NAFDAC before changing your formula, pack size or label, and keep your batch records ready to show.
The quality loop across channels
Make and code batch
Record where it went
Check shelves
Log feedback
Fix the cause
Each turn of the loop catches problems earlier, so fewer reach customers.
Stock rotation with partners

Use **FEFO: first expired, first out**. When you restock a shelf, move older jars to the front and put new ones behind. Shop staff often do the opposite because new cartons are easier to place at the front. Agree in writing that whoever restocks rotates the stock, and do it yourself during visits.
Check best-before dates on every shelf visit. Agree in advance what happens to stock within, for example, two months of its date: a promotion, a swap or collection.
Ask partners to store your product as your label says: for example away from direct sun, generators and hot shop windows.
Do not overstock. A shelf holding six months of sales ages your stock and ties up your money. Supply in smaller, more frequent drops.
The shelf check

Visit or ask for photos every two to four weeks. Use the same short checklist each time: Is the product on the shelf and visible? Is the price label correct and close to the RRP? Are any jars damaged, dusty or past date? Is stock rotated? How many units are left? Note the answers in your log. Remaining units also tell you **sell-through**, which you will use to decide whether to grow this channel.
Worked example: tracing a complaint
For example, a pharmacy in Garki tells Amaka that a customer returned a jar of shea butter that had separated and felt oily. The jar's code is SB-2409-02.
She thanks the pharmacy, offers the customer a replacement through the shop, and asks for a photo of the jar and where it was kept.
Her batch record shows SB-2409-02 made 60 jars: 24 to the Garki pharmacy, 24 to a Wuse salon and 12 sold direct.
She checks the shelf photo: the pharmacy displays jars in a window that gets afternoon sun.
She asks the salon and her direct buyers about that batch. No problems reported; the salon stores jars inside a cabinet.
Cause: heat exposure at one outlet, not the batch. She swaps the 9 jars remaining in Garki and agrees a new shelf away from the window.
One complaint, handled in two days, ended with a better shelf position and no wider recall. Without the batch code, she could not have shown that the other 36 jars were fine.
When it could be unsafe

If a complaint suggests a safety risk (a skin reaction, contamination, mould, a foreign object in food), stop supplying that batch, collect remaining units from all outlets that received it, and tell the customer to stop using it. For a regulated product, report it to NAFDAC. Speed matters more than embarrassment.
Returns and damaged stock

Agree a clear returns rule with each partner (see your agreement from Module 1). Typical points: damage on arrival reported within a short window is replaced by you; damage from poor storage at the shop is not; expired stock is handled as agreed. Record every return with the batch code and reason. Over a few months the returns log shows patterns, for example lids cracking in transit, which point to a fix in packaging rather than a dispute with a partner.

Finally, close the loop with your team. If the same question or complaint arrives twice from different outlets, put it on the agenda for your next production meeting. Quality problems found in distribution are often solved in the kitchen or the packing area.

To know which channels build your business, calculate what each one actually leaves you after the partner's share, fees, delivery and your production cost. Start from the shelf price and walk backwards. This is often called a **margin waterfall**.
An abacus for counting
Calculate each channel's true profit instead of assuming it.
Margin versus markup

Partners usually talk in **margin**: the share of their selling price they keep. Many small producers think in **markup**: what they add on top of cost. They are not the same. If a shop buys at 2,800 naira and sells at 4,000, it keeps 1,200 naira. As a margin that is 1,200 / 4,000 = 30%. As a markup it is 1,200 / 2,800 = 42.9%. When a shop says "we need 30%", ask: 30% of the shelf price, or 30% added to your trade price? The difference is real money.

When a distributor sits between you and the shop, both margins come out of the same 4,000 naira shelf price.

The retailer keeps 30% of 4,000 = 1,200, so it pays 2,800. A distributor that keeps 10% of its selling price to the shop keeps 280 of that 2,800 and pays you 2,520. Your cost of 1,900 leaves you 620 naira per jar. Selling the same jar direct for 4,000 would leave far more, but the distributor may sell hundreds of jars you could never reach yourself.
Fees and costs that hide in each channel

**Payment processing:** Paystack's published fee for local Nigerian transactions is 1.5% plus 100 naira, with the 100 naira waived under 2,500 naira and the total capped at 2,000 naira per transaction. Check the current rate before you calculate, since providers change prices.
**Marketplace fees:** commission and any fulfilment or listing fees vary by platform and category. Read the current rate in the seller centre; never guess.
**Delivery to partners:** the transport cost of a delivery divided by the units delivered.
**Agent commission:** a fixed amount or percentage per unit sold.
**Marketing:** for direct sales, divide what you spend on ads in a month by the orders they bring.

A shop owner's real question is not "is this product nice?" but "will it sell from my shelf and make me money without trouble?" Your pitch must answer that question with facts: who buys it, what the shop earns per unit, how reliably you deliver and what you do if something goes wrong.

A good pitch is a short business conversation backed by a one-page sell sheet.
Your sell sheet
A **sell sheet** is one page, printed and as a PDF for WhatsApp, that a buyer can keep. Include:
Product photo, name, sizes and the problem it solves for the customer, in one or two lines.
RRP, trade price and the shop's margin per unit in naira and as a percentage.
Minimum order, delivery area and lead time, payment terms.
Registration details where they apply (CAC number, NAFDAC number), batch coding and best-before.
Proof that it sells: approximate monthly sales, repeat customers, any outlets that already stock you (with their permission).
Your contact details and business account name.
The pitch pipeline

Small trial order

Move each outlet one stage at a time and record where every one stands.
List 10 to 15 outlets whose customers match yours: pharmacies, salons, gyms, mini-marts, gift shops.
Visit first as a shopper. Note similar products, their prices, where they sit and who decides what is stocked.
Ask for a short meeting with the decision maker, ideally at a quiet hour, not on a busy Saturday.
In the meeting: one sentence on the customer, show and let them try the sample, give the margin per unit, then offer a small trial.
Agree the trial in writing: quantity, price, terms and review date. Follow up the same day with the sell sheet and agreement.

A **trial order** lowers the buyer's risk: for example 12 units, with an agreement to review after 4 to 6 weeks. Some shops will ask for consignment for the first order. That can be reasonable for a trial, as long as the count dates and payment terms are written down.

Follow up without pestering. If a buyer says "come back next month", write the date in your pipeline and return on that date with something new: a stockist update, a customer review, or a fresh sample. Record every outlet's stage (target, visited, met, trial, regular) so you always know where your next order is most likely to come from. A "no" today is often a "not yet"; keep the door open politely.
Worked example: reading a trial
For example, Amaka lists 12 target outlets in Abuja, gets 5 meetings and 2 trial orders of 12 jars each, at a pharmacy and a gym.
Conversion: 2 trials from 12 targets is about 17%; from 5 meetings it is 40%.
After 4 weeks the pharmacy has sold 9 of 12 jars: sell-through 9 / 12 = 75%.
The gym has sold 3 of 12 jars: sell-through 3 / 12 = 25%.
The pharmacy reorders 24 jars on day 30. The gym makes no reorder and the jars sit behind the counter.
She asks the gym why. Members did not see the jars, and the staff could not answer questions about the product.

The pharmacy becomes a regular account. For the gym she offers a small shelf sign and a 15-minute staff briefing, with a second review in 4 weeks; if sell-through stays low she collects the stock and moves on.
Use each win to earn the next

With the partner's permission, mention current stockists in your next pitch and post where customers can buy you on your social media. Your direct channels can send buyers into shops, which helps those shops reorder.
Partnerships beyond wholesale
**Bundles and co-branding:** a body butter and a handmade soap from another maker sold together as a gift set, with costs and profits split in writing.
**Corporate and event gifting:** companies, hotels and event planners buying in bulk for staff gifts, guests or souvenirs, often with a custom label sleeve.

**Trade fairs and exhibitions:** events run by chambers of commerce, trade associations and women's business networks put you in front of many retail buyers in one day. Bring samples, sell sheets and a sign-up sheet for follow-up.
**Organisations that serve your customers:** cooperatives, associations or community groups that can introduce your product to their members.
Every partnership must still fit your brand standards and floor price. A gift set that requires you to cut quality or sell below your floor is a bad deal however famous the partner.
Avoid channel conflict
When you add partners in the same area, tell existing partners, keep price parity, and do not quietly offer a new shop better terms than a loyal one. Partners who discover that will feel cheated.

Agents and resellers can carry your product into estates, offices, churches, mosques and markets you never visit. They also carry your reputation. An agent who promises results your product cannot deliver, or who keeps customers' money, damages trust you spent years building. This lesson is about building an agent network that stays honest and productive.
A person teaching a small group
Agents sell better and more honestly when you train them properly.
Two ways to pay agents
Model
Best when
Commission
Agent takes orders and sends them to you or collects payment into your account; you deliver and pay the agent a fixed amount or percentage per sale
You want control of stock, cash and customer details
Reseller discount
Agent buys stock from you at a discount and resells at RRP, keeping the difference
Agents have their own capital and you want them to carry stock risk
Recruiting the right agents

Look for people who already talk to your kind of customer every day: a hairdresser, a pharmacy attendant, a fitness coach, a women's group leader, a busy office administrator. Ask for a referee who has known them for some time, take a copy of a valid ID, and record their phone number and home area. Start with three to five agents you can train and support well, rather than twenty you cannot follow up. A small, active network beats a long list of names who never sell.

Be honest in your recruiting message. Say what a realistic month looks like, for example "most agents sell 10 to 30 jars a month" only if your own records show that. Never promise income you cannot back with numbers, and never charge agents a registration fee to join; schemes that make money from recruiting people rather than selling products are a warning sign of a pyramid scheme.

Keep the terms the **same for every agent at the same level**. Negotiating differently with each person creates resentment when agents compare notes, which they will. You may reward high performers with a higher tier, but publish the rule: for example, 10% commission, rising to 12% for agents who sell more than 50 units a month.
The agent starter kit
Price list with RRP for each product and the agent's commission or discount.
A product facts sheet: ingredients, sizes, how to use, storage, and the claims agents may and may not make.
Approved photos and short captions for WhatsApp Status, plus the link to your WhatsApp Business catalog.
Answers to the ten questions customers ask most.
The order process, payment details for your business account, and a contact for complaints.
A 60-minute training session
10 minutes: the brand story and who the product is for.
15 minutes: hands-on with the product; each agent tries it and practises explaining it in their own words.
10 minutes: prices, commission and how orders and payments flow.
15 minutes: role play of common customer questions and one complaint.
10 minutes: stock, cash and safety rules; each agent signs the agent agreement.
Stock, cash and data rules

Customers pay into your business account or a payment link in your business name, never into an agent's personal account. Limit stock held by any new agent to a small amount until trust is built, and record every unit issued. Keep customer phone numbers and addresses private: agents must not add customers to groups or share their details without permission.

In shops, the staff who stand near the shelf decide whether customers hear about you. Leave a simple product card, brief staff in five minutes during restock visits, and tell them how to reach you with questions. Thank staff who report problems early.

Set up a short monthly call or WhatsApp voice note with your agents. Ask three questions: What sold? What did customers ask that you could not answer? What complaints did you hear? Record the answers. When the same comment arrives from several agents or outlets, take it to your production and packaging decisions. Part 3: the 90-day plan
A 90-day channel plan
Days 1-15: fix readiness gaps
Days 16-30: build pitch kit
Days 31-60: pitch and trial
Days 61-90: review and decide
Each phase has a clear output, so you can see in any week whether the plan is on track.
Worked example: Amaka's 90-day plan for pharmacies
For example, Amaka decides her next channel is independent pharmacies in Abuja, building on her first two branches.
Days 1 to 15: add a production day to raise capacity from 500 to about 600 jars a month; print batch codes; set aside 200,000 naira working cash for credit terms.
Days 16 to 30: update her sell sheet with current stockists (with permission) and the 30% shop margin; list 15 target pharmacies; prepare 15 sample jars.
Days 31 to 60: aim for 8 meetings and 4 trial orders of 12 jars; deliver within 3 days; first shelf check after 2 weeks.
Days 61 to 90: measure each outlet's sell-through, payment timing and true profit; hold a review with each one.
Targets: at least 3 outlets reordering, sell-through of 60% or more within 6 weeks, payments within the agreed 14 days, and a true profit of at least 750 naira per jar.
By writing the targets before she starts, Amaka knows exactly what success means. If she hits them, she adds a further 4 pharmacies in the next 90 days; if not, she studies why before spending more.
Decision rules at day 90
**Expand** when most targets are met: add outlets at the same pace your capacity and cash allow.
**Adjust** when sales are there but margin or payments are weak: renegotiate terms, change pack size, or shorten credit.
**Exit** when sell-through stays low after support and the channel uses more time and cash than it returns. Collect your stock politely and keep the relationship friendly.
Common mistakes to avoid
**Targets without numbers.** "Grow in pharmacies" cannot be judged at day 90; "3 outlets reordering" can.
**No cash plan.** Credit channels need working cash set aside before the first delivery, not after.
**Skipping the shelf checks.** Problems found in week two are cheap to fix; problems found in week ten have already cost you customers.
**Changing the product mid-trial.** If you change the recipe, jar or price during the 90 days, you cannot tell what caused the result.
**Forgetting existing customers.** Keep your direct buyers served and informed; they are still your most profitable channel.

If you plan to approach a bigger partner later, such as a supermarket chain or a regional distributor, your portfolio becomes your strongest argument. Show three things: steady sell-through at your current outlets, reliable on-time delivery from your order log, and enough capacity and cash to meet a larger order. Ask early for the partner's written supplier requirements, so your next 90-day plan can close those gaps one by one.
Keep the plan small
One new channel per 90 days, done well, usually beats three opened at once. Each new channel needs your attention during its first weeks, when most problems appear.

Present your portfolio and plan in a short document or a few slides with your brand colours. Keep supporting evidence in a folder: signed agreements, delivery notes, the order log, shelf-check photos and agent scorecards. This is the shift the course has worked towards: from selling a product yourself to running a brand that others help to sell, with the numbers to prove it is working.

For example, Amaka makes 250 g jars of whipped shea body butter in Abuja.
WhatsApp and Instagram, 260 jars
Market stall, 100 jars
One salon, 40 jars at 2,800

Before you add anything new, measure what you have. Amaka sells her jars directly for about 4,000 naira. Last month she sold 400 jars.
260 jars went through WhatsApp and Instagram. That is 1,040,000 naira.

If that account is hacked, most of her month is gone. Take your figures from your sales book or bank statements, not from memory.
Before you pitch
Product consistency: every batch the same
Packaging and paperwork: label, CAC, NAFDAC where needed
Capacity: extra units without starving buyers
Pricing headroom: profit left after their margin
Cash and admin: fund stock, invoice, keep an order log
Most new shop deals fail because the supplier was not ready. Score yourself 0, 1 or 2 on five areas.
One. Every batch looks, smells and performs the same.
Two. A finished label, CAC registration, and NAFDAC registration where your product needs it.
Three. You can make extra units without starving your existing customers.
Four. Your trade price leaves profit after the partner's margin.
Five. You can fund stock while you wait to be paid. A total of 8 to 10 means you can pitch. Below 8, fix your weakest area first.
Do the maths first
Can Amaka supply a pharmacy chain?
Never starve your loyal buyers. Protect existing demand first.
Chain asks: 4 branches x 24 jars x 2 = 192 jars
New total 592, but her maximum is 500
Cash tied up: 192 x 1,900 = 364,800 naira
Start with 2 branches: 96 jars, about 182,400 naira
A pharmacy chain with 4 branches asks Amaka for 24 jars per branch every two weeks. That is 192 jars a month.
Add her current 400 jars and she needs 592. But her kitchen and two helpers can stretch only to 500. She would be 92 jars short every month.
Each jar costs her about 1,900 naira to make, and the chain pays 30 days after delivery. So she must fund 364,800 naira of stock before the first payment comes.
So she starts with 2 branches. That is 96 jars, a total of 496, within her capacity, and about 182,400 naira of working cash.
Here is the rule. If a new channel takes stock your direct customers were waiting for, you swap a known, full-price buyer for an unproven, lower-price one. Protect them first, then add.
Price rules
Three price rules that protect you
Advise one shelf price, the RRP, so a customer sees roughly the same price wherever she shops.
Your lowest trade price, from cost. Cost 1,900 naira, 25% margin: 1,900 / 0.75 = about 2,533.
Do not sell online far below the shop price. Shop at 4,000, you at 3,200: the shop stops reordering.
First, set a recommended retail price, so a customer sees roughly the same price everywhere.
Second, set your floor price from your cost, not from a buyer's pressure. If a jar costs 1,900 naira and you need 25% margin, the floor is about 2,533 naira.
Third, keep price parity. If a pharmacy sells at 4,000 naira and you sell at 3,200 online, the pharmacy loses customers to you and soon stops reordering.
Who owns the stock?
Outright purchase or consignment
Outright purchase
The shop buys and owns the stock
Unsold units are the shop's problem
You know what you will be paid
You still own stock on the shelf
Shop pays only for what sells
Easier to get in, riskier for you
Write who pays for damage or loss
Outright purchase means the shop buys your stock and owns it. Unsold units are its problem, unless you agree otherwise.
Consignment means you still own the stock, and the shop pays only for what sells after each count.
It is easier to get in, but riskier for you, so write down who pays for damaged or missing units.
Put it in writing
Every agreement covers these six
If a term is not written down, each side remembers it differently. Amaka's one-page agreement said damage must be reported within 48 hours.
When a jar arrived cracked, that rule settled it in one message instead of an argument.
Key points
Remember
Measure each channel's share before adding a new one
Score readiness before you pitch; 8 to 10 means go
Calculate capacity and the cash credit terms tie up
Set an RRP, a floor price from cost, and keep parity
Agree terms in writing and know your walk-away point

To remember. Measure your channels from real records. Score your readiness, and check capacity and cash before you say yes. Set your prices from cost and keep parity. And put every agreement in writing, with your walk-away point decided before you negotiate.

Why this matters
A sale ends when the money is recorded
Order-to-cash: from order to money in your account
Unclear steps mean lost orders and forgotten invoices
One short written routine for each channel
Order-to-cash is the full path from the moment a partner orders to the moment the money is safely in your business account.
When any step is unclear, orders go missing, deliveries are disputed and invoices are forgotten. The sale is only finished when the money is recorded, not when the van leaves.
A short written routine for each channel prevents most of this. We call it an SOP, a standard operating procedure: a numbered list a helper can follow without asking you.
Step by step
An SOP for shop orders
Confirm every transfer in your banking app before releasing stock.
Confirm the order within 2 hours
Log it with an order number
Pick the oldest batch first, check labels
Delivery note and invoice with due date
Count together; both sign both notes
Remind one day before payment is due
Enter it in your order log with an order number.
Pick jars from the oldest batch first, and check each label and seal.
Prepare two copies of the delivery note, and an invoice showing the total and payment due date.
At delivery, count together with the shop staff, and both sign both notes. Without a signed note, quantities get disputed later.
One day before the due date, send a polite reminder. Record the payment the day it arrives.
And keep your money safe. Take payments only into your business account, never a helper's personal account. Fake transfer alerts are a common fraud, and never share your PIN or one-time passwords.
Your cash cycle
How long is your cash tied up?
10 September: 48 x 1,900 = 91,200 naira out
25 September: delivered, 15 days later
Net 30: paid 30 days after delivery
Cash cycle: 15 + 30 = 45 days
For example, Amaka makes shea body butter. On 10 September she spends 91,200 naira on materials for 48 jars for a distributor.
She makes and labels the jars, and delivers on 25 September.
The terms are net 30, which means payment 30 days after delivery.
So her cash cycle is 45 days. If the distributor pays 10 days late, it is 55. Before adding a second distributor, she checks she has enough cash for both cycles at once.
Quality on every shelf
Three quality habits
Code every batch, like SB-2409-02, and record where every unit went.
Older jars to the front, new ones behind. Supply little and often.
Every 2 to 4 weeks: visible, priced right, not damaged or past date, rotated.
In a shop far away, you cannot see a bad jar before a customer does. So, habit one: print a batch code on every jar, and keep a record of where each unit went.
Habit two: first expired, first out. Shop staff often put new cartons in front, so rotate the stock yourself on every visit.
Habit three: a shelf check every 2 to 4 weeks, using the same questions each time. The units left also show your sell-through.
Worked example
Tracing a complaint by batch
A jar from SB-2409-02 came back separated
Batch: 24 to Garki, 24 to a salon, 12 direct
Garki shows jars in a sunny window
No other complaints: heat, not the batch
A pharmacy in Garki says a customer returned a separated, oily jar. Amaka offers a replacement and asks for a photo.
Her batch record shows where all 60 jars of that batch went.
The shelf photo shows the jars in a window that gets afternoon sun.
The salon and direct buyers had no problems. So she swaps the 9 jars left in Garki and agrees a new shelf.
But if a complaint suggests a safety risk, like a skin reaction or mould, stop supplying that batch, collect it from every outlet, and for a regulated product report it to NAFDAC.
Margin waterfall
Walk back from the shelf price
For example, Amaka's jar sells for 4,000 naira through a distributor and a shop.
Shelf price
Retailer keeps 30%
Distributor keeps 10%
Her cost to make it
Naira prices are approximate.
A channel can bring big sales and still lose you money. So start from the shelf price and walk backwards.
The retailer keeps 30% of 4,000, which is 1,200, so it pays 2,800. That 30% is a margin, a share of the selling price. A markup is added to cost. Always ask which one a partner means.
The distributor keeps 280 of that 2,800, and pays Amaka 2,520.
Her cost is 1,900, so she keeps 620 naira per jar.
Look at the whole month
Profit per jar or profit per month
Per jar
Agent: 1,650 naira
Direct: 1,640 naira
Pharmacy: 800 naira
Distributor: 620 naira
Per month
Distributor, 300 jars: 186,000
Direct, 100 orders: 164,000
Plus your time and capacity
After fees, delivery, ads and commission, direct and agent sales leave the most per jar, and the distributor the least.

But the distributor might move 300 jars a month, for 186,000 naira, with no ads and no chatting. Direct sales stuck at 100 orders give 164,000. So compare total monthly profit, your time and your capacity.
Key points
Remember
Write a one-page SOP for each channel
Count your cash cycle in days
Code batches, rotate stock, trace complaints
Judge channels on true monthly profit

To remember. Write a short routine for each channel, and keep one order and payment log that you check every week. Count your cash cycle. Code every batch and rotate stock. And judge each channel on its true monthly profit, not on sales alone.

Why this matters
What a shop owner really asks
Will it sell from my shelf?
What do I earn per unit?
Will you deliver on time, every time?
What happens if something goes wrong?
A shop owner's real question is not, is this product nice? It is, will it sell from my shelf and make me money without trouble?
So your pitch answers with facts. Your one-page sell sheet shows the price, the trade price, and the shop's margin per unit in naira.
It also shows your minimum order, delivery time, payment terms, and proof that the product already sells.
Step by step
From target list to trial order
Agree every trial in writing: quantity, price, terms, review date.
List 10 to 15 outlets whose customers match yours
Visit first as a shopper; note prices and the decider
Ask for a short meeting at a quiet hour
Show the sample, give their margin, offer a trial
Follow up the same day with the sell sheet
Step one. List 10 to 15 outlets whose customers match yours: pharmacies, salons, gyms, mini-marts.
Step two. Visit first as a shopper. Note similar products, their prices, and who decides what is stocked.
Step three. Ask the decision maker for a short meeting at a quiet hour, not on a busy Saturday.
Step four. Let them try the sample, tell them what they earn per unit, and offer a small trial, for example 12 units, reviewed after 4 to 6 weeks.
Step five. Follow up the same day. And put the trial in writing. A no today is often a not yet, so return politely on the date they give you.
Reading a trial
Sell-through tells you what to do
Sold 9 of 12 jars in 4 weeks
Sell-through 75%
Reordered 24 jars on day 30
Gym
Sold 3 of 12 jars
Sell-through 25%
Jars sat behind the counter
Next: shelf sign, staff briefing

For example, Amaka sells shea body butter. She got trial orders at a pharmacy and a gym. Sell-through is the share of delivered stock that sells. The pharmacy sold 9 of 12 jars, which is 75%, and reordered.

The gym sold only 3, which is 25%. Members did not see the jars, and staff could not answer questions. So she offers a shelf sign and a 15-minute staff briefing. If sales stay low, she collects her stock and moves on.
Building a network
Recruiting agents the honest way
Pick people who talk to your customers daily
Take a referee and a copy of a valid ID
Start with 3 to 5 agents you can support
Same published terms for every agent
Never promise income or charge a joining fee
Agents carry your product into places you never visit, and they carry your reputation too. Look for a hairdresser, a fitness coach, a women's group leader.
Ask for a referee, take a copy of a valid ID, and record their phone number and area.
Start with three to five agents you can train well, not twenty you cannot follow up.
Keep the same terms for every agent at the same level, for example 10% commission, rising to 12% above 50 units a month.
Never promise income you cannot prove, and never charge a fee to join. Schemes that earn from recruiting people, not selling products, are a warning sign of a pyramid scheme.
Safety rules
Customers pay into your business account or payment link, never an agent's personal account.
Give new agents only a small amount of stock, and record every unit issued.
Keep customers' numbers and addresses private. No adding them to groups without permission.
Teach these rules in every training, and have each agent sign the agreement. First, cash: customers pay into your business account, never into an agent's personal account.
Second, stock: limit what a new agent holds until trust is built, and record every unit.
Third, data: customer phone numbers and addresses stay private.

Key points
Remember
